title: Ἀλέξανδρος ἐν θαλάμῳ
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Menelaus seizes Paris by the horsehair helmet and drags him toward the Achaean lines, the chin-strap choking him, until Aphrodite breaks the strap and the empty helmet comes away in his hand. He flings it to his companions and rushes back with his spear, but the goddess snatches Paris away in a thick mist and sets him down in his fragrant chamber. She then goes to fetch Helen from the tower, in the likeness of an old wool-dresser, and tells her that Alexander is waiting at home. Helen knows the goddess by her neck, breasts and eyes and bitterly refuses; Aphrodite threatens to abandon and ruin her, and Helen follows in silence. In the chamber she sits facing Paris and reproaches him for coming back alive, tells him to challenge Menelaus again, and then urges him not to. He answers that Athena helped Menelaus this time and calls her to bed. Meanwhile Menelaus ranges through the throng like a wild beast, and no one will show him Paris. Agamemnon declares the victory Menelaus’ and demands Helen, the possessions and a recompense; the Achaeans approve.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ ἐπαΐξας κόρυθος λάβεν ἱπποδασείης,
ἕλκε δ’ ἐπιστρέψας μετ’ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr:
ē kai epaïxas korythos laben hippodaseiēs,
helke d’ epistrepsas met’ eÿknēmidas Achaious·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and having rushed on, took hold of the helmet, horse-haired,
and dragged, having turned, among the well-greaved Achaeans;
sentences.i: So he said, and rushed on and caught hold of the helmet, thick with horsehair, and swung round, dragging him toward the well-greaved Achaeans;
sentences.n: Menelaus’ speech from the last part is over, and ἦ καί ‘he spoke, and’ starts the action: he rushes at Paris, whom the Greek does not name, and takes hold of his helmet (κόρυθος is a genitive after λάβεν ‘took hold of’). λάβεν and ἕλκε are past tenses without the augment, and ἐπαΐξας and ἐπιστρέψας are aorist participles. ἱπποδασείης ‘horse-haired, thick with horsehair’ agrees with κόρυθος and says that the helmet carries a horsehair plume, and ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς ‘well-greaved Achaeans’ is a stock phrase, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
ἄγχε δέ μιν πολύκεστος ἱμὰς ἁπαλὴν ὑπὸ δειρήν,
ὅς οἱ ὑπ’ ἀνθερεῶνος ὀχεὺς τέτατο τρυφαλείης.
sentences.tr:
anche de min polykestos himas hapalēn hypo deirēn,
hos hoi hyp’ anthereōnos ocheus tetato tryphaleiēs.
sentences.l:
and choked him the much-embroidered strap beneath his tender neck,
which beneath his chin as a fastening was stretched, of the helm.
sentences.i: and the richly embroidered strap choked him under his tender neck, the strap that was stretched beneath his chin as the helmet’s fastening.
sentences.n: The strap is the subject of ἄγχε ‘choked’, an unaugmented past of ἄγχω: as Menelaus drags the helmet, the chin-strap throttles Paris. ὅς is the relative ‘which’, ὀχεύς ‘fastening, holder’ says what the strap is for, and τέτατο is the pluperfect passive of τείνω ‘was stretched’. The sense of πολύκεστος is not certain; ‘richly embroidered’ is the usual explanation, from κεστός ‘stitched’. The origin of τρυφάλεια ‘helm’ is not known.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν εἴρυσσέν τε καὶ ἄσπετον ἤρατο κῦδος,
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη,
ἥ οἱ ῥῆξεν ἱμάντα βοὸς ἶφι κταμένοιο·
sentences.tr:
kai ny ken eiryssen te kai aspeton ērato kydos,
ei mē ar’ oxy noēse Dios thygatēr Aphroditē,
hē hoi rhēxen himanta boos iphi ktamenoio·
sentences.i: And now he would have dragged him off and won boundless glory, had Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, not been quick to notice; she broke the strap, which came from an ox that had been killed by force;
sentences.n: κεν with a past tense (εἴρυσσε, the augmented aorist of ἐρύω ‘drag’, with the doubled σ, and ἤρατο, the aorist middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’) says what would have happened, and εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε ‘if she had not sharply noticed’ says what stopped it. Διὸς θυγάτηρ ‘daughter of Zeus’ is her stock title. ἥ is the relative; ῥῆξεν is an unaugmented aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’; ἶφι ‘with force’ goes with κταμένοιο, an epic participle of κτείνω ‘kill’: the strap is ox-hide.

sentences.t: κεινὴ δὲ τρυφάλεια ἅμ’ ἕσπετο χειρὶ παχείῃ.
sentences.tr: keinē de tryphaleia ham’ hespeto cheiri pacheiēi.
sentences.l: but the empty helm came along with his thick hand.
sentences.i: but the helmet came away empty in his stout hand.
sentences.n: κεινή is Ionic κενή ‘empty’: the strap broke and the helmet came away without its wearer. ἕσπετο is the aorist of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ (Attic ἐσπόμην), and ἅμα … χειρί ‘along with the hand’ means it came off into his grip. παχείῃ ‘thick’ agrees with χειρί (‘thick’ in the literal line, ‘stout’ in the English line, as for the same two words in the Odyssey); the hand is Menelaus’.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν ἔπειθ’ ἥρως μετ’ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιοὺς
ῥῖψ’ ἐπιδινήσας, κόμισαν δ’ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι·
sentences.tr:
tēn men epeith’ hērōs met’ eÿknēmidas Achaious
rhips’ epidinēsas, komisan d’ eriēres hetairoi·
sentences.l:
That helm, for his part, then the hero among the well-greaved Achaeans
flung, whirling it round, and took care of it his trusty companions;
sentences.i: Then the hero whirled it round and flung it among the well-greaved Achaeans, and his trusty companions took care of it;
sentences.n: τήν is the helmet (τρυφάλεια is feminine), and the hero is Menelaus. ῥῖψ’ is the unaugmented aorist of ῥίπτω ‘fling’, and ἐπιδινήσας ‘having whirled round’ is a participle that gives the manner of the throw. κόμισαν ‘took care of’ says no more than that the companions saw to it. ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι ‘trusty companions’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ ἂψ ἐπόρουσε κατακτάμεναι μενεαίνων
ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ·
sentences.tr:
autar ho aps eporouse kataktamenai meneainōn
encheï chalkeiōi·
sentences.l:
But he, back again, rushed on, eager to kill him
with his bronze spear;
sentences.i: But he rushed in again, eager to kill him with his bronze spear;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ ἂψ ‘but he, back again’: ὅ is a pronoun, ‘he’. ἐπόρουσε is an unaugmented aorist ‘rushed upon’, and κατακτάμεναι is the epic infinitive of κατακτείνω ‘kill’ (the ending -μεναι is the old infinitive ending). μενεαίνων ‘eager’ is a participle, and ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ is a dative of instrument, ‘with a spear of bronze’. The unit stops mid-line at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐξήρπαξ’ Ἀφροδίτη
ῥεῖα μάλ’ ὥς τε θεός, ἐκάλυψε δ’ ἄρ’ ἠέρι πολλῇ,
κὰδ δ’ εἷσ’ ἐν θαλάμῳ εὐώδεϊ κηώεντι.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ exērpax’ Aphroditē
rheia mal’ hōs te theos, ekalypse d’ ar’ ēeri pollēi,
kad d’ heis’ en thalamōi euōdeï kēōenti.
sentences.l:
but him snatched away Aphrodite
very easily, like a god, and covered him then with thick mist,
and set him down in the sweet-smelling, fragrant chamber.
sentences.i: But Aphrodite snatched him away, with all the ease of a god, covered him in thick mist, and set him down in the sweet-smelling, fragrant chamber.
sentences.n: Aphrodite takes Paris out of the fight. ἐξήρπαξ’ is ἐξήρπαξε ‘snatched away’; ῥεῖα ‘easily’ and ὥς τε θεός ‘like a god’ are the poet’s comment that it costs a god no effort. ἠέρι is the dative of ἀήρ, which in Homer is mist, not clear air. κὰδ is κατά in tmesis with εἷσε, the transitive aorist ‘set down’ of ἵζω. θάλαμος is an inner room; εὐώδεϊ and κηώεντι both describe its scent, as ‘sweet-smelling’ and ‘fragrant’.

sentences.t: αὐτὴ δ’ αὖ Ἑλένην καλέουσ’ ἴε·
sentences.tr: autē d’ au Helenēn kaleous’ ie·
sentences.l: And she herself, in turn, Helen calling, went;
sentences.i: Then she herself went to call Helen;
sentences.n: αὐτή ‘she herself’ shows the goddess going in person on the errand. ἴε is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ (Attic ᾔει), and καλέουσ’ ‘calling’ is a participle that gives her purpose. αὖ ‘in turn’ marks the new step after the rescue.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ κίχανε
πύργῳ ἐφ’ ὑψηλῷ, περὶ δὲ Τρῳαὶ ἅλις ἦσαν·
sentences.tr:
tēn de kichane
pyrgōi eph’ hypsēlōi, peri de Trōiai halis ēsan·
sentences.l:
and her she found
on the high tower, and around her Trojan women in plenty were;
sentences.i: She found her on the high tower, with Trojan women crowded all around her;
sentences.n: τήν is Helen. κίχανε is an unaugmented past of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’, and πύργῳ ἐφ’ ὑψηλῷ ‘on the high tower’ is a dative of place. περί is an adverb, ‘around (her)’, and ἅλις ‘in plenty, in crowds’ says how many Trojan women (Τρῳαί, the edition’s spelling of Τρώαι) were there.

sentences.t:
χειρὶ δὲ νεκταρέου ἑανοῦ ἐτίναξε λαβοῦσα,
γρηῒ δέ μιν ἐϊκυῖα παλαιγενέϊ προσέειπεν
εἰροκόμῳ, ἥ οἱ Λακεδαίμονι ναιετοώσῃ
ἤσκειν εἴρια καλά, μάλιστα δέ μιν φιλέεσκε·
sentences.tr:
cheiri de nektareou heanou etinaxe labousa,
grēï de min eïkuia palaigeneï proseeipen
eirokomōi, hē hoi Lakedaimoni naietoōsēi
ēskein eiria kala, malista de min phileeske·
sentences.l:
With her hand she tugged, having taken hold of the nectar-sweet robe,
and to an old woman likening herself, of ancient birth, she spoke to her,
a wool-tender, who for her, as she dwelt in Lacedaemon,
was working fine wool, and most of all kept loving her;
sentences.i: She took hold of the robe, sweet as nectar, and tugged it with her hand, and spoke to Helen in the likeness of an old woman of great age, a wool-dresser who had worked fine wool for her when she lived in Lacedaemon, and had loved her most of all;
sentences.n: Aphrodite tugs at Helen’s robe, though the Greek gives no owner, and takes the form of an old woman: γρηΐ is the dative of γρηῦς ‘old woman’, after ἐϊκυῖα, the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’. παλαιγενέϊ ‘of ancient birth’ (literally ‘born long ago’) means of great age. εἰροκόμῳ ‘wool-dresser’ comes from εἶρος ‘wool’; she was Helen’s servant in Lacedaemon. φιλέεσκε is an iterative past, ‘kept loving’, and ναιετοώσῃ ‘dwelling’ is uncontracted. νεκταρέου ‘like nectar’ is the usual explanation.

sentences.t: τῇ μιν ἐεισαμένη προσεφώνεε δῖ’ Ἀφροδίτη·
sentences.tr: tēi min eeisamenē prosephōnee di’ Aphroditē·
sentences.l: Having made herself like to her, addressed heavenly Aphrodite:
sentences.i: Heavenly Aphrodite, making herself like her, spoke to her:
sentences.n: The speech introduction restarts after the description of the old woman. τῇ is the old woman, with ἐεισαμένη ‘making herself like’ (the aorist middle participle of εἴδομαι), and μιν is Aphrodite herself, the object of ἐεισαμένη (‘making herself like’), as in τῷ μιν ἐεισάμενος at 2.22; Helen, to whom she speaks, is not named in the line. προσεφώνεε is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω. δῖ’ is elided δῖα, ‘heavenly’, the stock epithet of Aphrodite, translated every time.

sentences.t: δεῦρ’ ἴθ’·
sentences.tr: deur’ ith’·
sentences.l: “Come here;
sentences.i: “Come here;
sentences.n: δεῦρ’ ἴθ’ is δεῦρο ἴθι: δεῦρο ‘here’ and the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’, an ordinary summons. The goddess speaks with the old woman’s voice, so that Helen will not know her, and the message follows in the next unit.

sentences.t: Ἀλέξανδρός σε καλεῖ οἶκον δὲ νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Alexandros se kalei oikon de neesthai.
sentences.l: Alexander calls you homewards, to go back.
sentences.i: Alexander is calling you to come home.
sentences.n: σε καλεῖ … νέεσθαι ‘calls you to go’: the infinitive says what he calls her to do. οἶκον δέ is οἶκόνδε printed as two words, ‘homewards’, with the suffix -δε of direction; νέεσθαι is the uncontracted present infinitive of νέομαι ‘go, go back’. Ἀλέξανδρος is Paris.

sentences.t:
κεῖνος ὅ γ’ ἐν θαλάμῳ καὶ δινωτοῖσι λέχεσσι
κάλλεΐ τε στίλβων καὶ εἵμασιν·
sentences.tr:
keinos ho g’ en thalamōi kai dinōtoisi lechessi
kalleï te stilbōn kai heimasin·
sentences.l:
That man there, in the chamber and on the round-wrought bedstead,
glistening in beauty and in clothes;
sentences.i: He is there in the chamber, on the bedstead worked in rounds, glistening in beauty and in clothes;
sentences.n: κεῖνος ὅ γ’ ‘that man there’, with ‘is’ left out. The picture is built to tempt Helen and says nothing of the fight. δινωτοῖσι ‘worked in rounds’ comes from δινέω ‘turn round’; whether the rounds are turned work or inlaid circles is not said, and the plural λέχεσσι is read as one bedstead. στίλβων ‘glistening’ is a participle of στίλβω, and εἵμασιν is the dative plural of εἷμα ‘garment’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κε φαίης
ἀνδρὶ μαχεσσάμενον τόν γ’ ἐλθεῖν, ἀλλὰ χορὸν δὲ
ἔρχεσθ’, ἠὲ χοροῖο νέον λήγοντα καθίζειν.
sentences.tr:
oude ke phaiēs
andri machessamenon ton g’ elthein, alla choron de
erchesth’, ēe choroio neon lēgonta kathizein.
sentences.l:
nor would you say
that he, having fought with a man, had come, but to a dance
was going, or from the dance having just ceased was sitting down.”
sentences.i: and you would not say that he had come from fighting a man, but that he was going to a dance, or had only just stopped dancing and was sitting down.”
sentences.n: οὐδέ κε φαίης ‘nor would you say’ is the optative with κε, ‘you would not think’. The infinitives report what you would think: ἐλθεῖν (aorist) ‘had come’ from a fight, and ἔρχεσθ’ and καθίζειν (present) ‘was going’, ‘was sitting’. μαχεσσάμενον has the epic double σ and takes ἀνδρί ‘with a man’; χορὸν δέ is ‘to a dance’, with -δε of direction; νέον ‘just now’. Aphrodite’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῇ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, tēi d’ ara thymon eni stēthessin orine·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and the heart in her breast she stirred.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and she stirred the heart in her breast.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so she spoke’ closes Aphrodite’s speech. τῇ is a dative of interest, ‘in her’, and it is Helen; θυμός ‘heart’ is what the goddess stirs; ὄρινε is a past tense of ὀρίνω without the augment. The same line stands in the Odyssey, there with a man as speaker and so ‘he’; the speaker here is Aphrodite, so ‘she’.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε θεᾶς περικαλλέα δειρὴν
στήθεά θ’ ἱμερόεντα καὶ ὄμματα μαρμαίροντα,
θάμβησέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr:
kai rh’ hōs oun enoēse theas perikallea deirēn
stēthea th’ himeroenta kai ommata marmaironta,
thambēsen t’ ar’ epeita epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l:
And when then she noticed the goddess’s very beautiful neck
and breasts full of longing and sparkling eyes,
she was struck with wonder then, and spoke a word, and called her by name:
sentences.i: And when she noticed the goddess’s very beautiful neck, her breasts full of longing and her sparkling eyes, she was struck with wonder, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: Helen sees through the old woman’s form by the goddess’s body. καί ῥ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε is ‘and when then she noticed’, with ῥ’ for ἄρα; θάμβησεν ‘was struck with wonder’ is an aorist. ἱμερόεντα ‘full of longing’ is built on ἵμερος ‘longing’ (breasts that stir longing), and μαρμαίροντα ‘sparkling’ on μαρμαίρω ‘flash’. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is a formula, ‘spoke a word and called by name’, with ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε in tmesis.

sentences.t: δαιμονίη, τί με ταῦτα λιλαίεαι ἠπεροπεύειν;
sentences.tr: daimoniē, ti me tauta lilaieai ēperopeuein;
sentences.l: “Strange woman, why do you long to deceive me in these things?
sentences.i: “Strange woman, why are you so eager to deceive me in this way?
sentences.n: δαιμονίη is the feminine vocative of δαιμόνιος, the address of one who finds the other’s behaviour baffling, ‘strange woman’. λιλαίεαι ‘you long’ takes the infinitive ἠπεροπεύειν ‘to deceive’, with με as its object; ταῦτα ‘in these things’ says in what. Helen speaks to the goddess as she is, having seen through the disguise.

sentences.t:
ἦ πῄ με προτέρω πολίων εὖ ναιομενάων
ἄξεις, ἢ Φρυγίης ἢ Μῃονίης ἐρατεινῆς,
εἴ τίς τοι καὶ κεῖθι φίλος μερόπων ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.tr:
ē pēi me proterō poliōn eu naiomenaōn
axeis, ē Phrygiēs ē Mēioniēs erateinēs,
ei tis toi kai keithi philos meropōn anthrōpōn·
sentences.i: Are you going to lead me still farther, to one of the well-inhabited cities of Phrygia or of lovely Maeonia, if some man there too is dear to you among men of articulate speech?
sentences.n: ἦ opens the question, and πολίων … ναιομενάων ‘of well-inhabited cities’ is a genitive depending on πῃ ‘somewhere’. ἄξεις is the future of ἄγω. Phrygia and Maeonia are lands of Asia Minor, and Helen’s sneer is that the goddess has another favourite there to give her to; τοι is σοι. The meaning of μερόπων is not known: ‘speech-dividing’, the ancient explanation, is followed.

sentences.l:
Because now heavenly Alexander Menelaus
having prevailed over wishes to take me, hateful, home with him,
for that reason now here, with guile in your mind, have you come to my side?
sentences.i: Is it because Menelaus has defeated heavenly Alexander and now wishes to take me, hateful as I am, home with him, that you have come to my side here, with guile in your mind?
sentences.n: οὕνεκα ‘because’ (οὗ ἕνεκα) and τοὔνεκα ‘for that reason’ (τοῦ ἕνεκα) answer each other, and the whole is one question, ending at the Greek question mark. νικήσας is a participle of νικάω ‘prevail over’; ἄγεσθαι is middle, ‘take with himself’, and στυγερήν ‘hateful’ is Helen’s word for herself. δολοφρονέουσα ‘with guile in your mind’ (δόλος ‘guile’ + φρήν ‘mind’); παρέστης is an aorist of παρίστημι, ‘you have come to stand beside’. δῖον ‘heavenly’ is Alexander’s stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἧσο παρ’ αὐτὸν ἰοῦσα, θεῶν δ’ ἀπόεικε κελεύθου,
μηδ’ ἔτι σοῖσι πόδεσσιν ὑποστρέψειας Ὄλυμπον,
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ περὶ κεῖνον ὀΐζυε καί ἑ φύλασσε,
εἰς ὅ κέ σ’ ἢ ἄλοχον ποιήσεται ἢ ὅ γε δούλην.
sentences.tr:
hēso par’ auton iousa, theōn d’ apoeike keleuthou,
mēd’ eti soisi podessin hypostrepseias Olympon,
all’ aiei peri keinon oïzye kai he phylasse,
eis ho ke s’ ē alochon poiēsetai ē ho ge doulēn.
sentences.l:
Sit beside him, having gone, and from the gods’ path give way,
and no more with your own feet may you turn back to Olympus,
but always about him suffer, and guard him,
until he makes you either his wife or he indeed his slave.
sentences.i: Go and sit beside him, and give up the path of the gods, and may you never again turn back to Olympus on your own feet; no, suffer for his sake always, and watch over him, until he makes you his wife, or else his slave.
sentences.n: Helen turns the errand back on the goddess: if she is so fond of Paris, let her go and live with him. ἧσο is the imperative of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and ἰοῦσα a participle of εἶμι ‘go’. ἀπόεικε, from ἀπείκω ‘give way’, takes the genitive κελεύθου ‘path’. μηδ’ ἔτι … ὑποστρέψειας is an optative used as a prohibition. ὀΐζυε is the imperative of ὀϊζύω ‘suffer woe’, ἑ is ‘him’, and ποιήσεται, middle, means ‘make for himself’.

sentences.t: κεῖσε δ’ ἐγὼν οὐκ εἶμι·
sentences.tr: keise d’ egōn ouk eimi·
sentences.l: But thither I will not go;
sentences.i: But I will not go there;
sentences.n: Helen’s refusal. κεῖσε ‘to that place’ means to Paris, ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ ‘I’, and the present εἶμι ‘I go’ has the sense of a future. The sentence is carried on by the two units that follow.

sentences.t: νεμεσσητὸν δέ κεν εἴη·
sentences.tr: nemessēton de ken eiē·
sentences.l: it would be a thing to resent;
sentences.i: that would be a thing to resent;
sentences.n: νεμεσσητόν is a verbal adjective of νεμεσσάω ‘feel resentment’: something that people would rightly resent. κεν with the optative εἴη means ‘would be’, and the English is the Odyssey’s for the same words. The remark is a parenthesis, and the thought of the previous unit continues in the next.

sentences.t: κείνου πορσανέουσα λέχος·
sentences.tr: keinou porsaneousa lechos·
sentences.l: that man’s bed to be tending;
sentences.i: to tend that man’s bed;
sentences.n: This goes with οὐκ εἶμι two units back: ‘I will not go there to tend that man’s bed’. πορσανέουσα is a future participle, of purpose, from πορσαίνω, a by-form of πορσύνω ‘prepare, tend’, and to tend a man’s bed is to share it.

sentences.t:
Τρῳαὶ δέ μ’ ὀπίσσω
πᾶσαι μωμήσονται·
sentences.tr:
Trōiai de m’ opissō
pasai mōmēsontai·
sentences.l:
and the Trojan women afterwards
will all find fault with me;
sentences.i: and afterwards all the Trojan women will find fault with me;
sentences.n: Her reason is shame before the Trojan women, the same Τρῳαί who stood around her on the tower (384). ὀπίσσω ‘afterwards’; μωμήσονται is the future of μωμάομαι ‘find fault with’, and μ’ is ‘me’.

sentences.t: ἔχω δ’ ἄχε’ ἄκριτα θυμῷ.
sentences.tr: echō d’ ache’ akrita thymōi.
sentences.l: and I have griefs, unsorted, in my heart.”
sentences.i: and I have endless griefs in my heart.”
sentences.n: ἄχε’ is ἄχεα, the plural of ἄχος ‘grief’. ἄκριτος is ‘unsorted’ (ἀ- + κρίνω ‘sort’), so ‘without distinction, without end’; the literal line keeps the first sense and the English line the second. θυμῷ is a dative of place, ‘in my heart’. Helen’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ χολωσαμένη προσεφώνεε δῖ’ Ἀφροδίτη·
sentences.tr: tēn de cholōsamenē prosephōnee di’ Aphroditē·
sentences.l: And her, enraged, addressed heavenly Aphrodite:
sentences.i: Then heavenly Aphrodite, enraged, spoke to her:
sentences.n: Aphrodite answers Helen as herself, in anger. χολωσαμένη ‘enraged’ is the aorist participle of χολόομαι, from χόλος ‘anger’; τήν is Helen. προσεφώνεε is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω, and δῖ’ ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
μή μ’ ἔρεθε σχετλίη, μὴ χωσαμένη σε μεθείω,
τὼς δέ σ’ ἀπεχθήρω ὡς νῦν ἔκπαγλ’ ἐφίλησα,
μέσσῳ δ’ ἀμφοτέρων μητίσομαι ἔχθεα λυγρὰ
Τρώων καὶ Δαναῶν, σὺ δέ κεν κακὸν οἶτον ὄληαι.
sentences.tr:
mē m’ erethe schetliē, mē chōsamenē se metheiō,
tōs de s’ apechthērō hōs nyn ekpagl’ ephilēsa,
messōi d’ amphoterōn mētisomai echthea lygra
Trōōn kai Danaōn, sy de ken kakon oiton olēai.
sentences.l:
“Do not provoke me, cruel one, lest, incensed, I abandon you,
and hate you as terribly as now I have loved you,
and devise grievous hatreds in the midst of both,
of Trojans and Danaans, and you perish by an evil fate.”
sentences.i: “Do not provoke me, cruel one, lest, incensed, I abandon you, and hate you as terribly as I have loved you until now, and devise grievous hatreds in the midst of both, hatreds of Trojans and Danaans alike, and you perish by an evil fate.”
sentences.n: One μή ‘lest’ governs the whole threat, a run of subjunctives: μεθείω (μεθίημι ‘let go’), ἀπεχθήρω (ἀπεχθαίρω ‘hate’; it could also mean ‘make hateful’), μητίσομαι (‘devise’; a short-vowel subjunctive, or else a future) and κεν ὄληαι (ὄλλυμι, middle ‘perish’). ἔρεθε is the imperative of ἐρέθω ‘provoke’, σχετλίη a vocative, ‘cruel one’, and χωσαμένη ‘incensed’ an aorist participle. ἔκπαγλα is the adverb ‘terribly’. Τρώων καὶ Δαναῶν are the peoples whose hatreds she threatens. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ἔδεισεν δ’ Ἑλένη Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα,
βῆ δὲ κατασχομένη ἑανῷ ἀργῆτι φαεινῷ
σιγῇ, πάσας δὲ Τρῳὰς λάθεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, edeisen d’ Helenē Dios ekgegauia,
bē de kataschomenē heanōi argēti phaeinōi
sigēi, pasas de Trōias lathen·
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Helen, the daughter sprung from Zeus, was afraid, and went, covering herself with the bright, shining robe, in silence, and escaped the notice of all the Trojan women;
sentences.n: Helen gives way. Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα ‘sprung of Zeus’, a perfect participle, is her stock epithet. βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω without the augment. κατασχομένη is the middle of κατέχω, ‘covering herself’, with the dative ἑανῷ ‘with the robe’, which ἀργῆτι ‘bright’ (ἀργής) and φαεινῷ ‘shining’ both describe. πάσας … Τρῳάς is the object of λάθεν, an unaugmented aorist of λανθάνω: ‘escaped the notice of’.

sentences.t: ἦρχε δὲ δαίμων.
sentences.tr: ērche de daimōn.
sentences.l: and led the divinity.
sentences.i: and the divinity led the way.
sentences.n: δαίμων ‘divinity’ is Aphrodite herself, who goes ahead of Helen; the Greek uses a masculine word for a goddess. ἦρχε is the augmented imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’.

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ ὅτ’ Ἀλεξάνδροιο δόμον περικαλλέ’ ἵκοντο,
ἀμφίπολοι μὲν ἔπειτα θοῶς ἐπὶ ἔργα τράποντο,
ἣ δ’ εἰς ὑψόροφον θάλαμον κίε δῖα γυναικῶν.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ hot’ Alexandroio domon perikalle’ hikonto,
amphipoloi men epeita thoōs epi erga traponto,
hē d’ eis hypsorophon thalamon kie dia gynaikōn.
sentences.l:
And when they came to Alexander’s very beautiful house,
the handmaids then quickly to their tasks turned,
and she to the high-roofed chamber went, heavenly-one of women.
sentences.i: And when they had come to Alexander’s very beautiful house, the handmaids quickly turned to their tasks, and she went into the high-roofed chamber, heavenly among women.
sentences.n: αἳ δ’ ‘they’ are Helen and her women (the feminine plural of the pronoun ὅ); the clause then divides them into ἀμφίπολοι μέν and ἣ δέ, so the goddess, who led the way at 420, is not counted in it. Which handmaids is not said; two had followed Helen to the tower (143–144). ἵκοντο is a past tense of ἱκνέομαι ‘come, reach’, and περικαλλέ’ is περικαλλέα ‘very beautiful’. ἀμφίπολοι ‘handmaids’ go back to their work, and τράποντο is an unaugmented aorist middle, ‘turned’. ὑψόροφον ‘high-roofed’ describes the chamber, and δῖα γυναικῶν ‘heavenly among women’ is Helen’s stock epithet.

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ ἄρα δίφρον ἑλοῦσα φιλομειδὴς Ἀφροδίτη
ἀντί’ Ἀλεξάνδροιο θεὰ κατέθηκε φέρουσα·
sentences.tr:
tēi d’ ara diphron helousa philomeidēs Aphroditē
anti’ Alexandroio thea katethēke pherousa·
sentences.l:
And for her a stool having taken up, smile-loving Aphrodite
opposite Alexander, the goddess, set down, carrying it;
sentences.i: Smile-loving Aphrodite, the goddess, took up a stool for her and, carrying it, set it down opposite Alexander;
sentences.n: The goddess carries the seat herself. δίφρος is a seat here, not the chariot of the last part. ἑλοῦσα is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take up’, ἀντί’ ‘opposite’ takes the genitive, and φιλομειδής ‘smile-loving’ is Aphrodite’s stock epithet, translated every time. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the second syllable of φιλομειδής is short by nature and has to be scanned long, as the first syllable of the fourth foot.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κάθιζ’ Ἑλένη κούρη Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο
ὄσσε πάλιν κλίνασα, πόσιν δ’ ἠνίπαπε μύθῳ·
sentences.tr:
entha kathiz’ Helenē kourē Dios aigiochoio
osse palin klinasa, posin d’ ēnipape mythōi·
sentences.l:
There sat down Helen, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus,
her eyes turning away, and her husband rebuked with a word:
sentences.i: There Helen sat down, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, turning her eyes away, and rebuked her husband in these words:
sentences.n: Helen sits down opposite Paris and turns her eyes away: ὄσσε is a dual, ‘the two eyes’, and the Greek gives no reason for turning them away. κάθιζ’ is a past tense of καθίζω ‘sit down’; κλίνασα, an aorist participle of κλίνω, ‘turning’; ἠνίπαπε a reduplicated aorist of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’, with μύθῳ ‘with a word’. κούρη Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο ‘daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t: ἤλυθες ἐκ πολέμου·
sentences.tr: ēlythes ek polemou·
sentences.l: “You have come from the war;
sentences.i: “You have come back from the war;
sentences.n: ἤλυθες is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι (Attic ἦλθες). Helen begins bitterly: he has come back from a fight that he has lost, and the next lines say what she wishes had happened. ἐκ πολέμου ‘from the war’.

sentences.t:
ὡς ὤφελες αὐτόθ’ ὀλέσθαι
ἀνδρὶ δαμεὶς κρατερῷ, ὃς ἐμὸς πρότερος πόσις ἦεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ōpheles autoth’ olesthai
andri dameis kraterōi, hos emos proteros posis ēen.
sentences.l:
would that you had perished there on the spot,
subdued by a strong man, who was my former husband.
sentences.i: if only you had perished right there, overcome by a strong man, who was my husband before you.
sentences.n: ὡς ὤφελες (ὀφείλω ‘ought’) with an infinitive is a wish that cannot now come true, ‘would that you had’. ὀλέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ὄλλυμι (middle ‘perish’), αὐτόθ’ ‘on the spot’, and δαμείς the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’. The strong man is Menelaus, whom Helen does not name; πρότερος ‘former’ is the word for her first husband, and ἦεν is ἦν.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν δὴ πρίν γ’ εὔχε’ ἀρηϊφίλου Μενελάου
σῇ τε βίῃ καὶ χερσὶ καὶ ἔγχεϊ φέρτερος εἶναι·
sentences.tr:
ē men dē prin g’ euche’ arēïphilou Menelaou
sēi te biēi kai chersi kai encheï pherteros einai·
sentences.l:
Truly indeed, before now, you were claiming than Ares-loved Menelaus
in your own might and hands and spear to be stronger;
sentences.i: Truly, before now you used to claim that you were stronger than Menelaus, dear to Ares, in your own might, your hands and your spear;
sentences.n: ἦ μὲν δή ‘truly indeed’ opens the sneer. εὔχε’ is εὔχεο, the imperfect of εὔχομαι, which with an infinitive means ‘claim’, not ‘pray’. The genitive Μενελάου goes with φέρτερος ‘stronger’, a comparison, and the datives βίῃ, χερσί and ἔγχεϊ say in what; σῇ is the possessive σός, ‘your own’. ἀρηϊφίλου ‘dear to Ares’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι νῦν προκάλεσσαι ἀρηΐφιλον Μενέλαον
ἐξαῦτις μαχέσασθαι ἐναντίον·
sentences.tr:
all’ ithi nyn prokalessai arēïphilon Menelaon
exautis machesasthai enantion·
sentences.l:
But go now, challenge Ares-loved Menelaus
again to fight, opposite him;
sentences.i: But go now and challenge Menelaus, dear to Ares, to face you again in a fight;
sentences.n: A dare, which she takes back in the next unit. ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’; προκάλεσσαι is the aorist imperative middle of προκαλέομαι ‘call out, challenge’, with the ending -σαι. ἐξαῦτις ‘again’; μαχέσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of μάχομαι ‘fight’; ἐναντίον ‘opposite, in person’. The edition prints the diaeresis in ἀρηΐφιλον.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά σ’ ἔγωγε
παύεσθαι κέλομαι, μηδὲ ξανθῷ Μενελάῳ
ἀντίβιον πόλεμον πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι
ἀφραδέως, μή πως τάχ’ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δουρὶ δαμήῃς.
sentences.tr:
alla s’ egōge
pauesthai kelomai, mēde xanthōi Menelaōi
antibion polemon polemizein ēde machesthai
aphradeōs, mē pōs tach’ hyp’ autou douri damēēis.
sentences.l:
but you I, for my part,
urge to stop, and not with fair-haired Menelaus
an opposing war to wage nor to fight
senselessly, lest perhaps soon by him with a spear you be subdued.”
sentences.i: But I, for my part, urge you to stop, and not to wage open war or fight fair-haired Menelaus senselessly, lest perhaps soon you be overcome by him with his spear.”
sentences.n: ἀλλά marks her turn from the dare to the plea. κέλομαι ‘I urge’ takes the infinitives παύεσθαι ‘to stop’ and, after μηδέ, πολεμίζειν and μάχεσθαι ‘not to wage war, not to fight’. πόλεμον πολεμίζειν pairs a noun and a verb of one root, as ‘wage war’ does; ἀντίβιον is ‘opposing’, ἀφραδέως ‘senselessly’. μή πως … δαμήῃς is ‘lest somehow you be subdued’, an aorist passive subjunctive of δάμνημι, with τάχα ‘soon’. ξανθῷ ‘fair-haired’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet. Her speech ends.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ Πάρις μύθοισιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.tr: tēn de Paris mythoisin ameibomenos proseeipe·
sentences.l: And her Paris with words, answering, addressed:
sentences.i: Paris answered her and spoke in these words:
sentences.n: Paris is the name used here for the man who is Alexander elsewhere in this part (421, 425); the poet uses both. The line is a formula: τήν is Helen, ἀμειβόμενος is ‘answering’ (ἀμείβομαι), and προσέειπε ‘addressed’.

sentences.t: μή με γύναι χαλεποῖσιν ὀνείδεσι θυμὸν ἔνιπτε·
sentences.tr: mē me gynai chalepoisin oneidesi thymon enipte·
sentences.l: “Do not, wife, with harsh reproaches rebuke my heart;
sentences.i: “Do not, wife, rebuke me to the heart with harsh reproaches;
sentences.n: μή … ἔνιπτε is a present imperative with μή, ‘do not rebuke’; the two accusatives με and θυμόν together say ‘me, in my heart’. γύναι is the vocative of γυνή ‘woman’, and from a husband to his wife it is rendered ‘wife’. ὀνείδεσι is the dative plural of ὄνειδος ‘reproach’, and χαλεποῖσιν ‘harsh’.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν γὰρ Μενέλαος ἐνίκησεν σὺν Ἀθήνῃ,
κεῖνον δ’ αὖτις ἐγώ·
sentences.tr:
nyn men gar Menelaos enikēsen syn Athēnēi,
keinon d’ autis egō·
sentences.l:
for now Menelaus prevailed, with Athena,
but that man again, I (shall prevail over);
sentences.i: for this time Menelaus has won, with Athena beside him, but I shall defeat him in turn;
sentences.n: γάρ gives his reason for asking her to stop: Paris credits Menelaus’ win this time to the goddess who was with him. ἐνίκησεν is the aorist of νικάω, here without an object, and σὺν Ἀθήνῃ means ‘with Athena’. The verb of the second half is left out, and one like ‘I shall prevail over’ is understood; κεῖνον is ‘that man’ and αὖτις ‘in turn, again’.

sentences.t: πάρα γὰρ θεοί εἰσι καὶ ἡμῖν.
sentences.tr: para gar theoi eisi kai hēmin.
sentences.l: for gods are beside us too.
sentences.i: for we too have gods at our side.
sentences.n: This is the reason for his confidence. πάρα … εἰσι is πάρεισι ‘are at hand’, with the prefix standing apart from the verb and its accent thrown back. θεοί is the subject, and ἡμῖν καί ‘for us too’ answers the Athena of the unit before.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ φιλότητι τραπείομεν εὐνηθέντε·
sentences.tr: all’ age dē philotēti trapeiomen eunēthente·
sentences.l: But come now, to love let us turn, having lain down, we two;
sentences.i: But come, let us turn to love, lying down together;
sentences.n: Paris’s answer is an invitation to bed. τραπείομεν is an aorist passive subjunctive of τρέπω ‘turn’ with the ending -είομεν for -ῶμεν, the same form as in the Odyssey’s ‘let us turn to bed’. εὐνηθέντε is a dual participle, ‘the two of us having lain down’, from εὐνάζω; φιλότητι ‘to love’ means making love.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πώ ποτέ μ’ ὧδέ γ’ ἔρως φρένας ἀμφεκάλυψεν,
οὐδ’ ὅτε σε πρῶτον Λακεδαίμονος ἐξ ἐρατεινῆς
ἔπλεον ἁρπάξας ἐν ποντοπόροισι νέεσσι,
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō pote m’ hōde g’ erōs phrenas amphekalypsen,
oud’ hote se prōton Lakedaimonos ex erateinēs
epleon harpaxas en pontoporoisi neessi,
sentences.l:
For never yet has desire so enfolded my wits,
nor even when you first from lovely Lacedaemon
I sailed, having snatched you, in sea-crossing ships,
sentences.i: For never yet has desire so enfolded my wits, not even when I first carried you off from lovely Lacedaemon and sailed in sea-crossing ships,
sentences.n: The sentence runs to 446 and is cut here at a comma because it is five lines long: οὐ … ὧδε ‘never so’ is answered by ὥς … νῦν ‘as now’. ἔρως ‘desire’ is the subject, and φρένας ἀμφεκάλυψεν ‘enfolded my wits’ the verb ἀμφικαλύπτω ‘cover round’. ἔπλεον ἁρπάξας ‘sailed, having snatched you’: the participle comes first in time. Λακεδαίμονος is a genitive after ἐξ, and ποντοπόροισι ‘sea-crossing’ is a stock word for ships.

sentences.t:
νήσῳ δ’ ἐν Κραναῇ ἐμίγην φιλότητι καὶ εὐνῇ,
ὥς σεο νῦν ἔραμαι καί με γλυκὺς ἵμερος αἱρεῖ.
sentences.tr:
nēsōi d’ en Kranaēi emigēn philotēti kai eunēi,
hōs seo nyn eramai kai me glykys himeros hairei.
sentences.l:
and on the island of Cranae I was mingled in love and in bed,
as now I desire you, and sweet longing takes hold of me.”
sentences.i: and on the island of Cranae I lay with you in love, as I desire you now, and sweet longing seizes me.”
sentences.n: νήσῳ δ’ ἐν Κραναῇ is ‘on the island of Cranae’, with ἐν standing between the two nouns; the poem does not say where Cranae is. ἐμίγην is the aorist passive of μίγνυμι ‘mingle’, used like an active, ‘lay together’. ἔραμαι takes the genitive σεο (= σοῦ), and ἵμερος ‘longing’ is the subject of αἱρεῖ ‘seizes’. Paris’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἄρχε λέχος δὲ κιών·
sentences.tr: ē rha, kai arche lechos de kiōn·
sentences.l: He spoke, and led the way, going to the bed;
sentences.i: So he said, and went to the bed, leading the way;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα, καί is the formula ‘so he said, and’. ἄρχε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’, κιών the present participle of κίω ‘go’, and λέχος δέ ‘to the bed’ has the suffix -δε of direction, printed as two words.

sentences.t: ἅμα δ’ εἵπετ’ ἄκοιτις.
sentences.tr: hama d’ heipet’ akoitis.
sentences.l: and with him followed his wife.
sentences.i: and his wife went with him.
sentences.n: ἅμα … εἵπετ’ is ἅμα … εἵπετο, the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ (with εἰ- for the augment ἐ-). ἄκοιτις is the plain word for ‘wife’. The poet gives Helen no further words: she obeys, as she did when she followed the goddess in silence.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐν τρητοῖσι κατεύνασθεν λεχέεσσιν,
Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἐφοίτα θηρὶ ἐοικὼς
εἴ που ἐσαθρήσειεν Ἀλέξανδρον θεοειδέα.
sentences.tr:
tō men ar’ en trētoisi kateunasthen lecheessin,
Atreïdēs d’ an’ homilon ephoita thēri eoikōs
ei pou esathrēseien Alexandron theoeidea.
sentences.l:
The two then in the bored bedstead lay down,
but Atreus’-son through the throng went to and fro, like a wild beast,
if anywhere he might catch sight of Alexander, godlike in form.
sentences.i: The two lay down in the corded bedstead, but the son of Atreus went to and fro through the throng like a wild beast, to see if he could catch sight of Alexander, godlike in form.
sentences.n: The scene changes to Menelaus. τὼ is a dual, ‘those two’, and κατεύνασθεν an aorist passive of κατευνάζω, ‘were laid to rest’, with the ending -θεν for -θησαν. τρητοῖσι ‘bored’: the frame was pierced for the cords that held the bedding. Ἀτρεΐδης is Menelaus here, ἐφοίτα ‘went to and fro’ ἀν’ ὅμιλον ‘through the throng’, and εἴ που ἐσαθρήσειεν ‘if anywhere he might catch sight of’ an aorist optative. θεοειδέα is Alexander’s stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ τις δύνατο Τρώων κλειτῶν τ’ ἐπικούρων
δεῖξαι Ἀλέξανδρον τότ’ ἀρηϊφίλῳ Μενελάῳ·
sentences.tr:
all’ ou tis dynato Trōōn kleitōn t’ epikourōn
deixai Alexandron tot’ arēïphilōi Menelaōi·
sentences.l:
But no one of the Trojans and the famous allies was able
to point out Alexander then to Ares-loved Menelaus;
sentences.i: But none of the Trojans or the famous allies could point Alexander out then to Menelaus, dear to Ares;
sentences.n: δύνατο is the imperfect of δύναμαι ‘be able’ without the augment, and δεῖξαι the aorist infinitive of δείκνυμι ‘show, point out’. κλειτῶν is κλυτῶν, ‘famous’, and goes with ἐπικούρων ‘allies’; Τρώων is ‘of the Trojans’. τότ’ ‘then’ is the time of the search; the next line says why no one helped.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γὰρ φιλότητί γ’ ἐκεύθανον εἴ τις ἴδοιτο·
sentences.tr: ou men gar philotēti g’ ekeuthanon ei tis idoito·
sentences.l: for not out of friendship were they hiding him, if anyone saw him;
sentences.i: for if anyone saw him, they did not hide him out of friendship;
sentences.n: γάρ explains: they were not shielding him as friends would. ἐκεύθανον is the imperfect of κεύθω ‘hide’, here with an extra -αν-, and εἴ τις ἴδοιτο ‘if anyone caught sight of him’ is an aorist optative middle, in a past general condition. φιλότητι is a dative of cause, ‘out of friendship’. The Greek states no subject; ‘they’ are the Trojans and allies of 451.

sentences.t: ἶσον γάρ σφιν πᾶσιν ἀπήχθετο κηρὶ μελαίνῃ.
sentences.tr: ison gar sphin pasin apēchtheto kēri melainēi.
sentences.l: for equally to all of them he was hateful as the black death-fate.
sentences.i: for he was as hateful to every one of them as the black spirit of death.
sentences.n: ἀπήχθετο is the aorist of ἀπεχθάνομαι ‘become hateful to’ (the stem has no nasal), with σφιν ‘to them’; ‘was hateful’ gives the sense. ἶσον … κηρὶ μελαίνῃ is a comparison in the dative, ‘equal to the black Ker’; κήρ ‘death-fate’ is a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’. The poet does not say why Alexander is so hated.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: toisi de kai meteeipen anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: And Agamemnon, lord of men, also spoke among them:
sentences.n: A speech introduction: τοῖσι ‘to them’ are the Trojans and their allies, and μετέειπεν is ‘spoke among’ (μετά + ἔειπε). ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the stock epithet of Agamemnon, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t: κέκλυτέ μευ Τρῶες καὶ Δάρδανοι ἠδ’ ἐπίκουροι·
sentences.tr: keklyte meu Trōes kai Dardanoi ēd’ epikouroi·
sentences.l: “Hear me, Trojans and Dardanians and allies;
sentences.i: “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians and allies;
sentences.n: κέκλυτέ μευ ‘hear me’ is the usual opening of a speech to an audience: κέκλυτε is a reduplicated aorist imperative and μευ the epic genitive of ἐγώ. Δάρδανοι ‘Dardanians’ are named beside the Trojans, and ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’ are the troops who fight for Troy but are not Trojans.

sentences.t:
νίκη μὲν δὴ φαίνετ’ ἀρηϊφίλου Μενελάου,
ὑμεῖς δ’ Ἀργείην Ἑλένην καὶ κτήμαθ’ ἅμ’ αὐτῇ
ἔκδοτε, καὶ τιμὴν ἀποτινέμεν ἥν τιν’ ἔοικεν,
ἥ τε καὶ ἐσσομένοισι μετ’ ἀνθρώποισι πέληται.
sentences.tr:
nikē men dē phainet’ arēïphilou Menelaou,
hymeis d’ Argeiēn Helenēn kai ktēmath’ ham’ autēi
ekdote, kai timēn apotinemen hēn tin’ eoiken,
hē te kai essomenoisi met’ anthrōpoisi pelētai.
sentences.l:
Victory indeed appears to be that of Ares-loved Menelaus,
but you Argive Helen and the possessions with her
hand over, and to pay back a recompense such as is fitting,
which shall be among men yet to come as well.”
sentences.i: Victory plainly belongs to Menelaus, dear to Ares, and you are to hand over Argive Helen and the possessions with her, and to pay a recompense such as is fitting, one that will remain among men yet to come as well.”
sentences.n: Agamemnon states the terms sworn in the last part, and 459–460 echo 286–287 there; 460 is word for word 287. φαίνετ’ is φαίνεται ‘appears’, with the genitive of the man whose victory it is. ἔκδοτε is the aorist imperative of ἐκδίδωμι ‘hand over’, and ἀποτινέμεν an infinitive standing for a command. τιμήν is the price paid for a wrong, ‘recompense’; Ἀργείην ‘Argive’ is Helen’s epithet. ἥ τε is a relative with epic τε. The speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀτρεΐδης, ἐπὶ δ’ ᾔνεον ἄλλοι Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ Atreïdēs, epi d’ ēineon alloi Achaioi.
sentences.l: So spoke Atreus’-son, and approved it the other Achaeans.
sentences.i: So spoke the son of Atreus, and the rest of the Achaeans agreed.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ closes the speech. Ἀτρεΐδης is now Agamemnon, as at 448 it was Menelaus: both are sons of Atreus, and the context says which. ἐπὶ δ’ ᾔνεον is ἐπῄνεον, the imperfect of ἐπαινέω ‘approve’, with the preposition standing apart. The Trojans do not answer in these lines.
